title: Missä: answering with -lla and -llä
summary: Missä can also be answered with -lla/-llä for a surface or a conventional at-location. Missä sinä olet? — Olen asemalla.
objectives: Use missä to ask about the taught at/on locations.
Answer with the appropriate -lla or -llä place form.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: Singular refers to one person or one thing in these patterns.
The inessive is the in-place form, answering where.
Missä can also be answered with -lla/-llä for a surface or a conventional at-location. The place word determines which family is natural; English at does not automatically mean -lla.
keyPoints: Do not change missä into mihin when the person or thing stays at the location.

sections.title: Answering the question
paragraphs: Use pöydällä (“on the table”), asemalla (“at the station”) and torilla (“at the market square”) in these taught contexts. A short location reply is natural. Keep the supporting person and verb forms shown in the question and intended reply.
A natural short reply to “Missä sinä olet?” is “Asemalla.” (“At the station.”). Use the full reply when it makes the person, action or correction clearer.
Reject the suggested location and then state the actual one. Negation does not turn an at-location into a from- or to-location.
The exercises show supporting Finnish words and their meanings when recalling them is not the task. Read the complete English meaning before choosing the question or answer form.
keyPoints: For these taught at/on places, use -lla/-llä rather than a from- or to-ending.

sections.title: Build the answer forms
paragraphs: asemalla means at the station here. Asema + -lla gives asemalla; this place conventionally uses the at/on family.
pöydällä means on the table here. Pöytä changes t to d before -llä: pöydä- + -llä gives pöydällä.
torilla means at the market square here. Tori + -lla gives torilla.
pihalla means in the yard here. Piha + -lla gives pihalla. Finnish uses this at/on family despite English in the yard.
tuolilla means on the chair here. Tuoli + -lla gives tuolilla.

steps: Missä: where; question asking where someone or something is. Missä is the inessive question form: it asks for the location, not a source or destination.
sinä: you; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Sinä addresses one person informally.
olet: you are; verb (the action or state). Olla has the singular you-form olet: ole- + -t.
Olen: I am; verb (the action or state). Olla has the I-form olen: ole- + -n. The ending identifies the speaker.
asemalla: at the station; at-location. Asema + -lla gives asemalla; this place conventionally uses the at/on family.

kirja: book; subject (who or what this sentence is about). Kirja is the basic singular form naming a whole book.
on: is; verb (the action or state). Olla has the irregular singular third-person form on.

steps: En: I do not; negative verb (marks not and identifies the person). En is the first-person singular negative verb. The main verb takes its negative form.
ole: be; main verb after the negative verb. After a present-tense negative verb, olla takes the unchanged form ole.
